question: A scene heading in a screenplay always includes:
option_a: Interior or exterior, the location, and the time
option_b: The camera angle and the lens

question: INT. in a scene heading means the scene takes place:
option_a: Inside

question: Action lines in a screenplay are written in:
option_a: Present tense

question: Which of these belongs in a screenplay's action line?
option_a: She checks the clock three times
option_b: She is anxious about being late
option_c: She remembers missing the bus last year

question: Why does 'He is furious but hiding it' not belong in a script?
option_a: A camera cannot record what someone feels, only what they do
option_d: It should be in past tense

question: A character's name above their dialogue is written:
option_a: In all capital letters, on its own line
option_b: In lowercase, inline with the dialogue
option_c: In italics at the end of the line
option_d: Only the first time they speak

question: A parenthetical tells you:
option_a: How a line is delivered

question: Parentheticals should be used:
option_a: Rarely, because if the line only works with one it should be rewritten

question: You need a new scene heading when:
option_a: The location or the time changes

question: Camera directions such as ZOOM IN or PAN LEFT belong:
option_a: On the shot list, not in the script

question: Screenplays are set in Courier because:
option_a: In Courier, one page runs about one minute of screen time
option_b: It is the easiest font to read
option_c: It is required by copyright law

question: A two column A/V script is a better choice than screenplay format for:
option_a: A documentary or a narrated promo
option_b: A short film with characters and dialogue
option_d: A project longer than three pages

question: In a two column A/V script, the two columns are:
option_a: Video on the left and audio on the right
option_b: Dialogue on the left and action on the right
option_c: Scenes on the left and shots on the right
option_d: Cast on the left and crew on the right

question: A storyboard shows:
option_a: What each shot looks like, one panel per shot
option_c: The order shots will be filmed in

question: A shot list is:
option_a: A table of every shot to get, with type, location, and equipment

question: A shot list is usually grouped by location rather than story order because:
option_a: You shoot everything in one place while you are standing in that place
option_c: The script is already in story order so it would be a duplicate

question: A call sheet tells the crew:
option_a: Where to be, when, and with what
option_c: How the project will be edited

question: A production schedule says:
option_a: What gets filmed on which day
option_b: How long the finished video will be
option_d: How the scenes are ordered in the story

question: Coverage means:
option_a: Shooting a scene from enough angles to have options when editing
option_b: Making sure the whole frame is filled

question: Continuity means:
option_a: Keeping details consistent across shots so the edit does not jump
option_d: Using the same lens for every shot

question: A table read is:
option_a: Reading the script out loud with people taking parts, to hear what works
option_b: A meeting where the schedule is set
option_c: Reviewing the storyboard as a group

question: The main reason to storyboard before shooting is:
option_a: So everyone on the crew pictures the same shot before a camera is involved
option_b: So the script can be shortened

question: A wide shot is most useful when you need to:
option_a: Establish where the scene is taking place

question: An over the shoulder shot is taken:
option_a: From behind one person, looking at another
option_d: With the camera on a moving vehicle

question: A cutaway is used to:
option_a: Cover an edit or add context by showing something else in the scene
option_d: Show the widest view of a location

question: CONT'D after a character's name means:
option_a: The same character is continuing to speak after an action line
option_b: The scene continues into the next page

question: If a script runs five pages when the assignment is three, the best fix is:
option_a: Find a scene that can be removed entirely
option_d: Move dialogue into the action lines

question: Dialogue in which two characters explain things they both already know is a problem because:
option_a: Real people do not talk that way, so it sounds false
option_b: It makes the script too short

question: Reading your dialogue out loud matters because:
option_a: Lines that look fine on the page often do not sound like a person

question: Using a different name for the same place in different scene headings (HALLWAY, then HALL, then MAIN HALL) is a problem because:
option_a: The crew and schedule treat them as separate locations

question: Before recording video, exposure should be set to:
option_a: Manual, so brightness does not drift mid-shot
option_b: Auto, so the camera adjusts as you move

question: The 180 degree rule says to set your shutter speed to:
option_a: About double your frame rate
option_c: The same as your frame rate
option_d: As fast as the light allows

question: You are shooting at 24fps. The correct shutter speed is about:
You are shooting at 30fps. The correct shutter speed is about:
Shutter speed is not used to control brightness in video because:
option_a: It is locked to the frame rate, so brightness is controlled with aperture and ISO instead
option_b: Shutter speed does not affect brightness

question: Autofocus is turned off for video because:
option_a: The camera hunts, racking focus in and out mid-shot, and that cannot be fixed later
option_c: Manual focus is sharper at every distance
option_d: Autofocus does not work in movie mode

question: White balance is set to a preset rather than auto because:
option_a: Auto shifts between takes, so footage will not match when it is cut together
option_b: Presets are more accurate in every situation
option_c: Auto white balance is not available in movie mode

question: Which of these CANNOT be fixed after the shoot?
option_a: Clipped audio
option_b: A shot that is slightly too wide
option_c: A file with a bad name

question: Room tone is:
option_a: 30 seconds of a location's ambient sound with nobody talking
option_b: A test tone played through speakers

question: When a shot is too dark, the correct order is:
option_a: Open the aperture, then raise ISO, then add light
option_b: Slow the shutter, then raise ISO
option_c: Raise ISO as high as it goes first
option_d: Slow the shutter below the frame rate rule

question: Raising ISO too far in video produces:
option_a: Noise, which is uglier in video than in a still photo

question: The best check before shooting anything real is:
option_a: Shoot ten seconds and play it back
option_d: Ask a classmate if the settings look right

question: Mixing frame rates inside one video is a problem because:
option_a: It causes playback and editing problems that are not worth the trouble
option_d: Audio will not sync to any of it

question: A memory card should be formatted:
option_a: In the camera, and only after everything is offloaded
option_b: On the computer before every shoot

question: A cut is:
option_a: Two clips placed back to back with no effect between them

question: The cut is used for the overwhelming majority of edits because:
option_a: It is invisible and does not interrupt, so time simply continues
option_b: It is the only free transition
option_c: It is the fastest to render

question: A dissolve tells the audience:
option_a: That time has passed, or that two things are connected

question: A fade to black usually signals:
option_a: That a chapter or section has ended

question: A wipe feels different from a dissolve because it is:
option_a: Deliberate and stylized, and the audience is meant to notice it

question: Putting a fancy transition between every clip is a mistake because:
option_a: It pulls attention away from the story and onto the editing
option_b: It takes too long to export
option_c: Software limits how many you can use

question: A typical dissolve lasts about:
option_a: 1 to 2 seconds

question: A J cut or L cut means:
option_a: The audio from one shot starts before, or continues after, the picture changes
option_b: The cut is made at a diagonal

question: The rule of thirds divides the frame into:
option_a: Nine parts, with the subject placed on a line or intersection

question: In a well framed shot of a person, the eyes usually sit:
option_a: Near the upper third line

question: Headroom is:
option_a: The space between the top of the subject's head and the top of the frame
option_b: The height of the ceiling in the location

question: Too little headroom makes a shot feel:
option_a: Cramped, as if the head is being cut off

question: Lead room is:
option_a: Space in front of where a subject is looking or moving
option_c: The distance the camera leads the subject
option_d: Extra footage before the action starts

question: A shot with no lead room feels wrong because:
option_a: The subject appears boxed in by the edge of the frame

question: Leading lines are:
option_a: Lines in the scene that pull the eye toward the subject
option_c: Guides shown in the camera viewfinder

question: Which of these could serve as a leading line in a school hallway?
option_a: A row of lockers running toward the subject
option_d: The length of the hallway in feet

question: Framing rules like the rule of thirds are best described as:
option_a: Defaults you can break on purpose for an effect
option_b: Laws that must never be broken

question: Breaking a framing rule by accident is different from breaking it on purpose because:
option_a: The audience cannot tell which you did unless the rest of the shot is clearly deliberate
option_b: Accidental framing is always more interesting
